This game is what the TES series used to be about.  You actually create a character (not just pick their face and a name), and get to explore a living world.  Factions aren't such generic affairs either that anyone can join.  To be in the mages guild, you ACTUALLY HAVE TO BE A MAGE.  Not simply rolling a mage class (you are free to make any custom class you want), but actually have magic skills leveled up and some mage-like attributes.  No brain dead orcs that can only cast the most basic of cantrips will ever rise up and lead the mages guild.  Also, you couldn't just join every faction.  If you become a member of hte Imperial Cult, the native Tribunal Temple will see you as a heretic and turn you away at the door.  However, if you join the Fighter's Guild, you'll find members of House Redoran hold you in better esteem: the two factions respect the skill and good works the others do.  Conversely, the Telvanni see the Mages Guild as rival upstarts and you'll have the opposite problem.  Raise too high in their ranks and Telvanni peasants will spit on you and their merchants refuse you business.  HOWEVER you can always increase your personality and practice a little speechcraft to overcome these problems! 

See, Morrowind was a much more inolved game.  You have so much more control over who your character is and the world will actually react to your choices.  Skyrim took huge steps backwards in this respect.  What was actually far more engaging is the interplay between skills and attributes.  Each skill is governed by an attribute, and raising those skills was the main way of raising those attributes.  So that orc earlier will gain strength from bashing people over the head with his hammer and spending time repairing his own armor.  The mage will gain gain willpower controlling powerful arcane energies and intelligence from spending time brewing his potions and enchanting his gear.  There were no warriors spending all day clubbing shit on the head and spontaneously generating more magicka points on level up... And once again, even with the class system there was nothing stopping a warrior from becoming a mage.  ESPECIALLY since the magic system wasn't built around absurdly high costs reduced through perks and equipement... it meant magic hybrids were far more viable, especially as there were more support skills.  Like a warrior that uses absorb health/strength skills to weaken his foes while he strengthens himself and collect the souls needed to power his enchanted equipment... and enchanting was even better.  Enchanted items could hold spells, like healing or lock picking, that could help non-mage characters access more of the game. So the aforementioned warrior could keep his enchanted gear in top form from collecting souls in the wild to power his lock picking ring or fire-ball flinging guantlets he needs to fight off ghosts. 

But enough about that.  The every atmosphere of morrowind was far better.  The whole island just feels alien and is begging to be explored.  It felt like around every corner was some ancestral tomb filled with ghosts and vampires, a smugglers den filled with skooma and diamonds, or some deadric temple filled with crazed cultists.  And more importantly, these places had much more organic layouts.  What I mean is, that in Skyrim 99.9% of dungeons were all designed to be long hallways.  Even the old forts and such were structured, with collapsed tunnels and barrickaded one-way doors, to be just one giant twisting hallway.  That temple isn't a temple, its one giant hallway.  That fort? Also a hallway.  That cave? Also a hallway.  And 90% o the time, they wrapped around to the beginning.  So that long twisting daugr ruin/cave? Just so happens that behind the main chamber is a lever, that opens a door, that opens right to the entrance EVERY TIME.  Combined with the brain dead "puzzles" of throwing a lever right in front of a locked door, and it just feels too gamey.  You never really get the feeling you are actually exploring an abondoned temple... but instead just plowing straight through another 'level" in the game.  

And just to hammer home how timeless the game truly is, its 15 years old and still getting mods.  One was added this very day, and the day before that, and the day before that.  And if no mods are being added, older ones are being updated.  You have thousnds of mods across 15 years to sample from.  So what are you waiting on, jump in!

Morrowind is, without a doubt, one of the greatest RPGs ever created. The sense of exploration and character progression is difficult to match even in modern games. I played Oblivion and Skyrim when they came out, and neither game gripped me as much as Morrowind did.

I'm not a "quest markers are for babbys" person, but the lack of objective markers, the need to pay attention to a map, stumbling into random people, settlements, caves, random encounters, etc makes this game special.

Morrowind was my first proper RPG, and I was way too young to understand what it was asking of me. I was about six when it came out, playing it on the old cream-coloured family PC with one of those massive CRT monitors. The game barely ran. I borrowed the base game and the expansion packs from a childhood friend, back when we still called them expansion packs instead of DLC, and it absolutely blew my mind.

I did not really understand quests at all. The idea of reading a journal and actually using my brain to work things out was a bit much for six year old me, so I mostly ignored the main story. But that did not matter. I spent hours and hours just existing in the world. Wandering around, levelling terribly, murdering random NPCs, robbing shops, clearing dungeons, and generally doing whatever I felt like. I must have sunk hundreds of hours into Morrowind without ever really “playing it properly”. Because of that, I have a huge amount of nostalgia for it. I eventually went out and bought my own copy from Gamestation in the UK, and I still own that copy today. Good old boxed PC-ROM games you actually had to install.

That said, I still genuinely think it is an excellent game, even now. I have completed it a few times properly since I was a child, and it still holds up incredibly well. My Steam playtime is only my most recent playthrough, which I have barely even touched, and it still does not come close to how much time I have really spent in this game over the years. If you like RPGs, can tolerate older games, and are not completely fried by modern hand-holding design, Morrowind is absolutely worth playing. It is a proper sit down, get lost, and have an adventure kind of game.

There is also an insane amount of content. The main quest alone is substantial, but it is only a small part of what the game offers. Guild questlines, Great House factions, Daedric quests, random caves, ruins, and side stories are everywhere. You can play for dozens of hours without touching the main story at all, and that is not even counting Tribunal and Bloodmoon, which add huge chunks of extra content on top. The world feels dense and deliberately paced rather than bloated, and almost everything feels meaningful to engage with.

Josh Strife Hayes summed it up perfectly. Skyrim is basically an action game with some RPG bits tacked on. Oblivion sits somewhere in the middle. Morrowind is one of the last true RPGs, with just a little bit of action layered on top. Your stats matter. Your build matters. Dice rolls matter. The world does not care if you are confused or lost. You can fail badly and mess up your character or even your entire playthrough beyond repair. People hear that now and think it sounds like bad design, but honestly, that is part of what makes it so great. It does not treat you like you are stupid, and everything you achieve feels genuinely rewarding in a way modern games rarely manage anymore.

Yes, it has flaws. The graphics are obviously dated, even if they still hold up surprisingly well for their age and art style. The levelling system is weird and poorly explained. The game is completely unapologetic about not holding your hand. There are no quest markers, no glowing paths, no constant reminders telling you exactly where to go. There are loads of mods, and the modding scene is incredible, but I would strongly recommend doing at least one mostly vanilla playthrough first, the way the game was intended. After that, go wild. There are mods out there that overhaul systems, massively improve visuals, and add hundreds of hours of extra content.

Instead of holding your hand like you are an idiot, the game tells you to talk to people, explore, and figure things out. Someone will say “go south-west from this town, past a rock, near the coast, and look for a cave”, and that is the entire quest log. When you finally find the place or the item, it feels genuinely rewarding because you did it yourself, not because you followed an icon on a map. It really is one of the last truly great RPGs ever made.

If you have never played Morrowind and you enjoy, or want, a real RPG experience, love The Elder Scrolls in general, or have any interest in the Dunmer and their weird, alien land and lore, you absolutely should give it a go. It demands patience, but it gives a lot back in return, and almost everything you do feels genuinely earned.

Though this is actually the 3rd game in the Elder Scrolls series, I feel that this is the game that actually put the series into the mainstream. The original graphics have not aged well, but the fact that the game is mod-able means that even now you can get a visual treat from this game. Vvardenfell is full of fantastical and beautiful visuals, though they may not be as polished as Skyrim. The imagination and execution of the alien settings in the game are masterful. The immersion this game allowed was downright revolutionary for its time. The story was deep and the game itself was a challenge. Be aware that there are many areas in the game where, if you are not high enough in level, you will easily get destroyed. In that sense, the game also provided a realism that is lost in the more modern aspects of the series. Yet you could also become a god via skillful manipulation of the game's deep and satisfying skill system. The story is engaging and rewarding. Characters are a bit bland, but mostly that is the game showing its age at this point. A great game overall.

Playing the game now, it feels very dated. But I still really enjoy it. My favorite way to play the game as an adult is to create a character and give myself rules for how that character would act. I'm currently playing an "honest" Nord that won't kill (unless provoked) or steal. It forces me to change up the way I normally "exploit" my own knowledge of the game when making a new character.

And the game can be easily exploited. It feels like cheating when you understand how the mechanics work and where to find all the good loot. Creating rules for myself as I play (to avoid exploiting the game a bunch) has helped me enjoy the game again. I've even discovered a love for questing (one I didn't have at all when I played it as a teenager).

I love this game in spite of its flaws and I think I always will.

Morrowind has the most complex map design and world-building ever made.

Numeric and objective explanation of this FACT. Morrowind has:

1.-The biggest locations density ever included in a videogame. 70 [i]settlements[/i] -sedentary cities, towns and villages, ashlander camps, houses and farms- near 400 "dungeons", and other enterable places -caves, mines, dwemer ruins, daedric ruins, ancestral tombs, etc-, and 100-200 other locations -ships and shipwrecks, imperial forts, landmarks, etc- and a total of more than 1.000 enterable spaces!  That means far more locations and [i] interiors[/i] than Skyrim or Witcher 3, e.g., in a truly smaller map.

Not counting open empty waters, the land area is [i]only[/i] about  1.100 cells or 15 sq Km approx. Seems a lot bigger isn't it? This is because an intelligent landscape design -all the hills and slopes, the not-visible content from distance even with "distant land" enabled, because landform, etc.- and obviously because the enormous quantity of content too. No other videogame in History reachs the Morrowind’s =~50 places per sq Kilometer… nor the =~75 enterable spaces -interiors- x sq Km.

Indeed, sometimes we can experience some portions of the landscape as [i]barren[/i] or some regions as [i]uninhabited[/i] (an illusion!) being actually full of locations, objects and npcs -as no other  game- and this is only possible with a landscape design as MW has.

So summarizing: Focus on detail and more content >>>> Bigger maps.

2.- The most complex, mature, credible society ever put in a virtual environment. 34 clearly in-game factions, 11-15 of them joinable. The largest amount of original books in a single player game -more than 200 of the 300 total-. An extremely diverse, coherent architecture with at least 14-15 totally different styles, that represent the main socio-politic divisions or pieces of a distant History, and every style with a enormous amount of diversity. 

Many internal interests, conflicts, traditions or status presented or not by dialogue, architecture or books are present too in subtle details as clothes, names, etc.  Two examples of these subtle world details: 1º Some ashlander-camp dialogue explains you how some old ashlanders left the traditional lifestyle and became sedentary velothi, living with other common dunmers, and some time later you'll begin to link and understand how exist some settlement where the majority of the inhabitants shares personal naming conventions not with other sedentary dunmers but with ashlanders, and this settlement -I won't spoil too much- is the only one of the Vvardenfell towns with a large ashlander style tent too... 2º. Clothes have a highly detailed information of the world. Some clothes are exclusive of specific factions or professions as the different Ashlander tribes, the Morag Tong or Tribunal Temple robes, well that was good but not so special, but in some clothes as these two last specific robes some little decorative texts in daedric script add cryptic messages… that if you learn the Daedric Alphabet can transcript  as mottos relative at their owner occupation! And these details are only presented for world building consistency, without practical, story or quest dependency. When you begin to discover or even "suspect" these hundreds of details, the immersion is complete, as in no other video game ever.

3.- 2.700 UNIQUE npcs. The largest number of npcs ever included in a single player game. MW has more unique npcs than every other Elder Scrolls -the other 7 non online- + the whole "The Witcher" series put together!  With the dlc’s, the unique npcs count reachs near 3.000. Of them more than 1.700 are “friendly” npcs and the rest are hostiles. Every unique npc have a personalized combination of face/hair -[i]only[/i] 1300 archetypes, enough to be "G.o.a.t."-, apparel, name, level,  attributes, skills, class/profession,  spells, faction and rank, inventory and owned things, etc. 

The dialogue -about 30.000 lines- exist in shared and unique forms. The unique dialogue is mostly associated with quests, with some exceptions in relevant npcs. The total number of unique npcs owning  different dialogue including quest-related is still larger than most games. Certainly is simple dialogue, without particulary good writing. However Morrowind dialogue is not simply "wikipedia dialogue" as critics claim, not only because the shared dialogue is filtered by a big quantity of factors and topics, usually having more than one answer depending on who and where you ask and these new answers not only adding information but presenting sometimes another point of view, but most importantly because there are subtle details that even in the shared/common dialogue makes Morrowind great. For example, most hostile npcs have their own dialogue if you calm them, mostly generic dialogue, but some have unique dialogue or even they can be trainers or merchants, so if you calm them and have a good disposition, you could use their “services”… because hostile npcs “are people too”… Not many games share [i]world consistence[/i] features like that.

4.-Another brilliant Morrowind’s accomplishment is the originality of the fantasy world building, although tolkienesque altmer/bosmer names, imperials=pseudo-romans or nords=vikings wasn't too original, the totally new creation of the Dunmer and their homeland -not present at Morrowind form in the precedent games-, was something completely different.

The main cultural inspirations moved from "pseudo-medieval-western-Europe" to a strong mesopotamian and ancient middle east influence -from toponimy, ashlander names, dunmer temples and cantons to some hlaalu architecture and cities, dwemer ghost looks, sacred triads, etc.-, some sort of japanese stylized art –besides katanas-, N. America first nations or eurasian steppes. These inspirations could be cool by themselves, but then, a miriad of really innovative aspects were inserted in the Dunmer tradition, and the D&D cliché of the Dark Elves was transformed into a really new people, with a totally innovative aspects and an alien culture, the Dunmer: The traditional nomadic herders, the ashlanders confronted with their sedentary Velothi cousins, the  ideology and culture of the Telvanni, the original and severe Redoran world, the speculative religious lore about the existence and the possibility of transcend the simply mortal condition, the Dwemer people, this atheistic-scientific reclusive people with a steam-punk-Assyrian vibe and their mysterious vanishing,  of whom we only know by their enemies, the egg-mines, the silt striders and the rest of the insectoid-reptilian big fauna, the Kwama life cycle, the Sixth House, the living gods, these floating zigurats, and the floating moon, the moon sssugarrr, the skooma and the new foods, the never well explained aspects but still very present in the world -the Dunmer Strongholds, the Velothi towers, the common Velothi folk non affiliated to any Great House-, etc. 

I could add 3-4 points more, but the steam space limitations prevent me from doing.

In every aspect, Morrowind is not exactly a “masterpiece” in the sense of "perfection" -being the most perfect yet in most the aforementioned features, still is only a "beginning"-, but the pioneer in most of open world features. Morrowind is the definitive step -after some Ultima, and specially Darklands and Daggerfall- in the definition of a total different genre, the Open World experiences, the simulated worlds, [i]virtual realities[/i].

Let's be clear: Morrowind has absolutely dated graphics and animations. There’s no voiced dialogue, no quest markers, no responsive AIs, and fast travel is limited at best. Does that make it a pain to play today? Perhaps. It's a world remarkably alien and bizarre compared to classic fantasy RPG concepts.

Yet this exact world feels so real, so alive, and tells a main storyline less epic than none. A game that opens with a dream and hands you a passport to an enchanted, uncaring, and unapologetically dense world. It sucks you into it, forcing you to read, think, and explore---to actually become part of this world---in order to progress. It asks you not to conquer it, but to [i] understand [/i] it. 

The spirit of TES always went beyond mechanics and graphics. It was about the world that speaks back to you in whispers. But the names that once gave it that soul---MK, Ken, Jeremy Soule, and now Kurt---are gone. Under the Xbox acquisition, I don't know if BGS can still find the experimental spirit and layered worldbuilding they once had, rather than going for mass-market appeal. Now, there [i] is [/i] a community that remembers, and there are indie developers carrying the flames. But to make a big open-world game this vast and complex, I can only imagine the compromises a small studio would be forced to make.

VI might still surprise us. I hope it does. But right now, I feel that a spiritual successor to Morrowind may never come from Bethesda. It might come from someone who loved it as much as we do, somewhere else.

Honest 10/10, has to be one of the best games ever made.

PROS

 - Best TES game in terms or lore, storyline, environment, and immersion, also most challenging by far
 - Magic is much more complicated than in the later TES games, you can make your own spells and basically become a God, you can also levitate, which is a lot more fun than running
 - There's dozens of hours worth of in-game books, as well as a very well documented UESP section for Morrowind, which can help you on quests, character building, etc. (http://en.uesp.net/wiki/Morrowind:Morrowind)
 - The narrative doesn't feel rushed like Oblivion or Skyrim, and you are part of an ancient struggle as opposed to a melodramatic invasion
 - The graphics are dated, but with MGE you can mod them to be on par with a game from the late 00s. My  modded game looks almost as good as SSE, although I use a few texture packs.
 - Only a few mods can greatly update the graphics and melee combat (use the Morrowind Sound and Graphics Overhaul, or just use MGE and install your own textures like I do, although this is more difficult to someone new to modding)
 - The Game doesn't hold your hand and you can't just play on max difficulty the whole time, also most enemies and NPCs are at a static level, meaning you can't kill the main boss at level 10 like in Skyrim.
 - The community is still active and makes some pretty dank memes on YouTube. (https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PL7En5ohTjD_X_1ry7kKoblLPDknNYlNEx)

CONS

 - The graphics were good for 2002, but not so much anymore. A few mods can fix this quite easily.
 - Combat is outdated, but can be fixed with a small mod.
 - The game can be iffy on Windows 10 in my experience, but it's mostly stable (more so than Skyrim for me).
 - The game has a bad max resolution (something under 1600x900, which isn't even full HD) which can only be fixed by MGE to my knowledge.

ADVICE:
 - Use the Accurate Attack mod to "fix" the vanilla melee. It's an easy fix to the number one issue that turns people away from the game.
 - Use the UESP pages to read up on strategies to the game to help you with quests and the like. It's a lot harder to just derp through Morrowind than Skyrim or even Oblivion.

Overall an absolute classical legend of a game. Buy it.

[h1]My Friend Morrowind[/h1]
[u]A Personal Reflection about Why Games are Important[/u]

The game that has most been on my mind lately is [b]Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind.[/b] I've found myself humming the main theme a few times in the past month or so, and I always feel a saturated pulse of remembered emotion.

I first played Morrowind on the original xbox, which I kept alive for years past a natural end using a soldering iron and a dream.  It was a dark time for me, Atlanta in 2000s.  I was working 60-80 hours a week tending bar and barely pulling in enough to pay for my studio apartment, my cats, my phone, my food, an occassional xbox or ps2 game, and enough booze to suppress my as-yet-undiagnosed mental illness.

I would get home in the wee hours of morning and play Morrowind, often falling asleep on the couch with controller in hand.  It wasn't the story, exactly, though the story is not bad.  My life was so painful, and I felt so little control over my circumstances- until I entered Morrowind.  

[h1]Three central characteristics made the game so perfect for my needs.[/h1]  

[b]First, the player-guided, emergent, pseudo-sandbox nature of the game's narrative.  I could go anywhere and attempt anything, ignoring or engaging the "main plot" however I saw fit.[/b]  I remember little about that storyline and I kept playing my character for hundreds of hours after its completion.  In Morrowind, I had agency over my choices, and I improved at the things I chose to do.  When I felt unable to change my world or myself, when I felt unfit for my own goals and dreams- this aspect of Morrowind grew profound, became deeply important to me.

[b]Second, the enormous and diverse cast of characters.[/b] So many scripted characters going about their own business for their own reasons. So many stories to be told by the many individuals, so many books to be found and read in the world.  Morrowind felt populated by real people, so to speak.  Many of the characters have simple tales to tell that illustrate the vicissitudes and banality and struggle of everyday life.  This is a world in which everyone toils through their labors day by day, whether a hero comes or not.  I saw my life through the lens of toil, and I was comforted.

[b]Third, the sheer alien-ness of the world-building.[/b]  This is not your typical white-washed, messianic fantasy of a hero's journey set in an idealized medieval Europe.  This is Morrowind, and only Morrowind.  The Elder Scrolls have returned to a more mainstream fantasy vision and I believe they are weaker games for it.  Every step taken in the game was a journey of discovery of new and stranger wonders, and I was in love with each new one.  What better place to find solace from our world than in a world so alien to my expectations?

When I catch that music in my head and I get that thrill through my body, that wash of emotions from an immensely upsetting time, I reflect on Morrowind with a sense of deep gratitude for the role it played in my life.  In fact, the experience profoundly affected the way I understand and interact with video games, elevating the process from recreational narrative experience to [b]important literary medium[/b] and even [b]beloved and faithful friend.[/b]

What can i say, Morrowind is possibly one of the greatest RPGs ever made. Though it can be a little buggy and is a little unstable at times without some mods, it offers countless hours of exploration, interesting characters and enjoyable quests. 

I'll state that it can be a little difficult the first time round, as the learning curve is a little steep and your starting stats play a huge factor in the challenges you'll face. Quick travel is also only available from certain areas, via boats, spells and Silt Riders. This may seem a little obtuse to Oblivion/Skyrim/Fallout fans, but I personally believe it's the better system. It results in the player actually exploring the world and discovering the services available, and arguably makes the world seem more "alive". There is also no compass marker pointing directly towards your objective, which means you need to read listen to directions properly and read your journal if you lose track of anything. You know, like a real adventurer...right?

There is also a way of maximising stat rewards by training skills my certain amounts and in a certain order, which is made easier by being able to pay for training anytime you wish, as long as you can find the trainers. Unlike Oblivion/Skyrim, which has a Five time cap per level, you can train endlessly per level. So it rewards focus on primary attributes such as Strength skills, Agility skills and Personality skills etc.

[b]Top Tip:[/b]
Combat can be daunting and infuriating, due to it's reliance on simulated dice rolls, but if you spec your character correctly, you can overcome issues and upsets that many new players face. Starting as the Redguard race, with Long Blade, Athletics and Block as 'Major Skills', and selecting The Steed as your 'Birth Sign' will give you what you need to take on most early combat scenarios and will ensure you aren't walking incredibly slowly around the world.

One who has been introduced to the series late will usually ask himself the following question, "Is Morrowind still worth playing today?"
To put it simple, yes. Without a doubt. I am ready to say that it is worth playing much more than any other game in the Elder Scrolls series.

Many people started with Oblivion, but I wouldn't be surprised if a majority started with Skyrim, whereas Morrowind is sometimes left into obscurity by many due to the game being too hard at lower levels, and people never touch it again because they couldn't take the time to understand the mechanics and how to level up abilities properly.
Some do not bare with the fact that you have to actually look for stuff, properly explore and read your quests and quest log and follow directions rather than follow an arrow on their map that tells them where to go at all times.

Fact is, compared to later installments in the series, Morrowind is much richer both in RPG elements and lore.
Oblivion still had a fair amount of RPG elements in them but many we're taken out, whereas Skyrim has abandonned the RPG genre completely and turned itself into an action-adventure game with skill progression.

No fast travel? No problem! If you walk a road, any road really, there's a 95% chance that you will encounter a dungeon or an NPC that has a quest for you, making exploration meaningful and fun. You can travel by boat or silt strider between cities, though, and you can also teleport using scrolls, spells or enchanted items.
Many of those quests will give you items that are usually of relevance, whatever your class is, even artifacts sometimes, and there's a ton of them, so there's no time to get bored or run out of stuff to do.

The magic system is incredibly rich. There are literally hundreds of differents spells. And I don't mean Fireball 10 damage, 20 damage and 30 damage counts as 3 spells, No. Hundreds of different spells at your disposition, whether it be fire, frost, poisonous or shock damage, fortify aptitudes, water walking, summoning the dead, healing the wounded and curing diseases, turning invisible, forging shields and proper defensive mechanisms against every situation, levitation, telekinesis, unlocking chests and doors, command and charm others, turn people crazy, paralysis, jump really really high, trap your enemies behind doors and cast locking spells on said door, destroy the weapons and armors of your enemies, the list goes on and on. You can even make your own spells, combining several effects. How awesome is that?

Do you like lore? Prepare to be delighted, as Morrowind has tons, tons, TONS of lore. Relevant books with extensive and detailled dialogues with NPCs, you can literally spend hours reading the numerous tomes available in libraries if that's your thing.
Remember voice acting in Oblivion and Skyrim? Pretty pathetic and shallow, wasn't it? 
Morrowind has little voice acting, meaning that the few voice acting it had actually had effort put into it, and since the dialogue is text based, there is much more information than you would usually get with voice acting, and the little voice acting there is in the game is actually enjoyable for once, even with regular NPCs. 
Here's a good example of guards in the city of Vivec throwing insults at you or acknowledging your presence, if you are curious ; https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RIPAEoRr9JA

There's a few remarks I hear often about Morrowind, here's a few ;
-"The game is broken" : Every single Bethesda open world game is broken. Every single one of them. Please name one that is stable. Protip ; You can't.
-"Morrowind is abusable" : If you know what you're doing, yes. If you're playing casually for the first few times and don't know where the artifacts are, not neccesairly.
Oblivion is abusable, Skyrim is abusable, and it's much easier to learn how to properly abuse in those two games than in Morrowind. 
Hell, Skyrim has a list of over-powered perks at your disposition when you level up. 100% invincibility when you sneak, slow down time by 50% and zoom in with your bow, lockpicks never break, heavy armor that doesn't affect your speed and weight, not to mention the dragon shouts.
-"The graphics are very bad" : This game was made in 2002. A 2002 game with that much content and detailing was very impressive for the time, but yes, it doesn't look very good for today's standards. 
You are free to download Morrowind Overhaul, a complete set of visual mods that makes the game much prettier and pushes the engine to it's very limits. Be sure to have a more than capable system, though. The mod is optimized for several types of rigs, from low-end to high-end, but if you want the most out of it, you need a good computer.
-"I can't hit anything with my sword" : Morrowind is an RPG. Let's say you are using long swords with a skill of 5 in Long Swords, which is the minimum skill level. 
A level this low pretty much means that your character never held a sword in his hands, therefore, your hit rate is extremely poor. The higher your skill, the higher your hit rate, the higher chance you have to hurt your target.
Your major skills are the key when you are doing a fresh game. You are born with those skills so you must use them accordingly to your advantage. 
If you want to use magic but you've chosen the preset class "Fighter", don't try to throw spells untrained at level 1. You're a Fighter, not a Mage.
If you wish to learn how to use other skills later on, you are free to pay various trainers to train any skills and use them on your own when you are good enough to adventure in the wild. This is how RPGs have worked since the very beginning of Dungeons & Dragons and how they are supposed to work, the genre has only been simplified over the years to attract a broader, and shall I say weaker audience to make more money off casual players.
-"If I hit someone with a sword in real life, he will be hurt" : Most likely, but Morrowind is an RPG, not real life. Refer to point above.
-"There's a cliff racer every two minutes" : There's a dragon in Skyrim every five minutes. A fight with a cliff racer lasts ten seconds, a fight with a dragon lasts five to ten minutes. Yeah, yeah, we all had that epic feeling when we killed our first Skyrim dragon, but it gets exceedingly repetitive after 10 of them, and the sole purpose of most dragon fights is to be time consuming.

I am fully aware that Morrowind is not for everyone. Most gamers nowadays do not want to take the time to properly learn how to play a game with more depth and difficulty than they can handle after 30 minutes of gameplay.
For hardcore RPG fans, those who like a challenge, freedom in a world that is rich in content, those who like to experiment with custom enchants and custom spells, 
those who enjoy insane amounts of interesting lore, extensive lists of skills to level up, an interesting map to explore with various architectures and landscapes, and hundreds amongst hundreds of hours of gameplay for literally peanuts, this game is for you.
I've been playing Morrowind for 13 years, played Oblivion at release and Skyrim at release, and I've played all three extensively, plus a little bit of Daggerfall on the side. 
I hold little nostalgic feeling to this game compared to many other games I can think of, so don't play the "Nostalgia" card on this review, because it does not apply.
Despite this, there is only one Elder Scrolls title that I truly enjoy coming back to every time.

With the direction the video game industry has been taking in the past several years, despite it's numerous flaws, there is absolutely no doubt in my mind that, [i]In my opinion,[/i], Morrowind is still and will most certainly always be the greatest 3D Elder Scrolls title to be ever released.
Take your time with it, level up carefully, learn how the game is played and managed, sink several hours into it, deal with the difficulty curve, learn from your mistakes in the game and keep on going. 
Trust me, it's worth it.

Morrowind may have not aged well with its clunky combat, dumb AI and poor animations, and while mods can improve on many of its flaws, it will still be hard to get into it for those that started with Skyrim. However, if you give it a chance you will discover that there's a lot more to it. 

Exploration is rewarding, bits and pieces of lore are hidden and scattered around the map and not every detail of the story is laid out in front of you, and discovering it on your own is part of the experience. The lore is intertwined with the plot.

Magic will open a world of possibilities. Want to enchant a pair of boots that will make you jump over mountains? You can do it. Want a pair of pants that shoot fireballs? No problem! Alchemy, Enchanting and Spellmaking will turn you into a god in no time, experiment different combinations and you will feel like you can do anything.

Skyrim is a bloody good game, but it has given up a lot of the older TES freedom for a balanced and polished gameplay. Morrowind isn't polished or balanced in any way, but that's actually what makes it special: it's a giant playground where your creativity is the only limit.

The best in the series in gameplay and creativity but not in graphics. However, what does someone expect from a game that's this old? I'll keep it simple as I don't want to start the comparing apples to apples crud. 

Pros: 
- EPIC score! The music is the best out of the series and where TES got it's legendary beat. All TES musical projects after this game reflect Morrowind's in some small way. 
- "Break me if you can" mentality. This game let's you break it with spell creation and enchantments. You want a very specific spell or enchantment? This game let's you create that perfect one if you have the correct build. Once made a spell that let me fly everywhere all the time when I was 14. Nearly shat the water walking pants I found in game. Then made a spell that kills me instantly. Why? Literally because I could. 
- Weapons are extremely extensive. Longswords? Check. Shortswords? Check. Hammers? Ding. Staffs? Yep. Spears? Affirmative. Bows? Roger that. Throwing weapons like "ninja stars", darts, and knives? Damn straight. Hand to hand? Extremely satisfying, oddly. 
- Character creation. You can make some seriously out there classes with this creator. Want to play as nothing but a Bard that does nothing more than sing and make money at taverns with no real combat skills? Oh yeah, this game let's you do that and much more. 




Cons:
- As soon as you get outside to the main meat of the game you have NO hand holding. This game treats you like an adult right off the bat. You figure it out. No quest markers, nothing but a map, journal, and your wit. 
- Reading. Loads and loads of reading comes into play here. Only seriously main characters speak with voiced dialogue and even then it can be rare. Also you NEED to read everything. Skipping over somewhat menial could have drastic consequences. 
- Graphics did not age well at all. This looks like a game straight out of the early 2000's. Character creation is also a con somewhat as there are not many looks to choose from, but vary just enough to where different save profile characters will more or less look different, if not funny sometimes. 
- Combat is atrocious! You may look like your hitting your opponent but you will more often than not wonder why you're not causing damage. This is because it's all based on dice roll instead of just mashing LMB to win. If you suck at swordfighting then don't try getting into a swordfight. You will get owned. 
- Saving. MAKE SURE YOU SAVE! Save file corruptions can be rampant sometimes.

[h2]Hard to get into, rough around the edges, but still worth playing in 2026[/h2]

If you are looking to experience this game for the first time, here's three things that might help:

[b]1) Get the openMW project and use that to run your game.[/b]

It's easy to set up and will be more stable on modern hardware, while also running smoother.
It's also supports a lot of mods.

[b]2) Get your reading glasses and get comfy. There is a lot of text.[/b]

Only a few lines in the game are voiced.
Quests have a lot of text, which will give you clues on possible solutions, locations and additional sources of information. Check your journal, check the dialogue options with NPCs, read books and letters.
You really have to read a ton, if you want to keep up with your tasks and the main story.

[b]3) Don't go full murder-hobo. Or do, I'm not your real Mom.[/b]

If you kill certain NPCs, the main quest will not be able to progress, even if the NPCs are no longer required for the story. You will still be able to "finish" the main quest, but you will no longer be able to experience the journey to the finale. If you get a message after you killed an  NPC, it's best to reload.
Likewise, you can find non-critical NPCs out in the wild, some who even attack you, who are important to side quests. If you want to rank up in the factions.
Killing them before you get the quest can sometimes lead to a bad quest outcome later on. 

Overall, the game is mechanically and visually dated, but the journey from "zero to hero" is very addicting, once you get into it. And there's a huge world to explore, full of opportunities to get side-tracked.
I recommend starting your first character with at least one weapon skill in your major skills, so you can hit stuff.
The best faction questline to start with, is the Temple's quest imo. 
It shows you a lot of the world, provides a challenge and gives you some cool rewards.

A true no frills adventure game. I cannot highly recommend it enough. A few points to follow though -

1) Download mods. Please do not play this without them and expect a great experience. Don't turn yourself away from the game right away. It's nearly 20 years old at this point, the game could use all the help it can get.

2) Take it easy. There's no wrong way to play. There are certainly "sub-optimal" builds for your character, but that's the fun of the game. You want to swing a big ass mace and cast spells in light armor? Go for it.

3) Don't look everything up. The directions that the NPCs give you for a quest are given that way on purpose to encourage exploration and discovery. Taking the long way to your objective is infinitely more rewarding, both in material rewards as well as in the enjoyment you'll get from this carefully constructed world. That leads me to the next point.

4) Look up, look down, look all around. There's loot behind tapestries, under pillows, behind beds. EVERYWHERE. Most of it is a little gold or potions, but some of the best items the game has to offer are hidden in locations you'd never go to normally. Harking back to point number 3, explore. It's a vast open world out there and the island of Vvardenfel holds many secrets at the tops of towers and depths of the many caves.

5) Ask the community. Morrowind has a fan base stretching back 20 years now. If you need advice or just want to learn more about the game, we're here. If you have a second monitor, I usually watch Lyle Shnub's Morrowind Mondays playthrough while pitter pattering my way around Vivec.

With Skyrim getting yet another release, I feel like there's no better time to look to some of the older games and appreciate them for what they are and embrace that lost sense of storytelling Morrowind has to offer.

Good luck out there Outlander, and watch out for the Clffracers!
